chapter: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
title: Origins of the Ellington sound: Miley and Irvis
summary: The sound grew from Bubber Miley's plunger trumpet and Charlie Irvis's trombone, giving the Jungle Band style.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Certainly Johnny did make a contribution. So did you and so did many of the instrumentalists in the orchestra. You were talking about sort of the line of development of the Ellington sound a few minutes ago.
Yes, the Ellington sound is a development over many years, or -- and many influences. I believe -- I joined the band in '32, so it had been developed quite a bit

when I got there. But there seemed to be two or three influences that were the strongest, and one of the influences was the influence of a trumpet player by the name of Bubber Miley and a trombone player by the name Charlie Irvis.

Bubber Miley was a person who played with a plunger, and different mutes and got different effects. And Irvis was did the same thing on trombone, and the two of them were like a duo, and it sort of developed that they were a jungalistic type of music. Then the band became the accompaniment to this music.

At one time the band was called The Jungle Band, and the basis of the later and larger band all seemed to revert back to this jungle and this way of jungle playing, until finally it dissolved itself into a pattern of new way of playing, a sort of a melodic jungle, melodic way of playing. All developed from one thing to another to another, and that way, till finally it wound up what it finally became.
